title: Environmental history: people, nature and the Great Acceleration
examples: How much has carbon dioxide risen?

explain.say: In 1958 the scientist Charles David Keeling began measuring carbon dioxide in the air on Mauna Loa, a volcano in Hawaii. Look at the real curve: about 316 parts per million in 1959, about 421 in 2023. Before the industrial age it was about 280. One careful daily measurement became one of history's most important documents.

draw.text: Environmental history: people, nature and the Great Acceleration

explain.say: So what is environmental history? See two directions. Nature shapes people: Alfred Crosby showed how European germs, animals and weeds helped conquer the Americas. People reshape nature: William Cronon showed how colonists changed New England's land. Which direction do you notice more in your own region?

Watch the chain. Fossil fuels powered industry and cars. After 1950 population, energy use, fertiliser, dams and plastics all shot up together, which historians John McNeill and Peter Engelke call the Great Acceleration. Some scientists name our era the Anthropocene, the age of humans. Which link would be hardest to change?

Disasters sparked movements. Look at the timeline. The London smog of December 1952 killed thousands. Mercury poisoning hit Minamata in Japan, Rachel Carson's Silent Spring warned of pesticides in 1962, and the Bhopal gas leak in India in 1984 killed thousands. Laws and campaigns followed. Why do disasters often come before change?

explain.say: Look at the map. Environmental history is global: India's Chipko women hugged trees to stop logging in 1973, Wangari Maathai's Green Belt Movement planted millions of trees in Kenya, and the Amazon shapes the world's climate. Environmental justice asks who bears the harm. Great work. Challenge: find one environmental change in your town's history.

faq.a: The study of how people and the natural world have shaped each other over time: climate, disease, soils, forests, energy and pollution, and how societies understood and fought over nature. Leading historians include Alfred Crosby, William Cronon and John McNeill.

The sharp, simultaneous rise after about 1950 in population, energy use, economic output, fertiliser use, dams, plastics and carbon emissions, described by John McNeill and Peter Engelke. Many scientists link it to the idea of the Anthropocene.

faq.q: How much has carbon dioxide risen?
faq.a: Measured at Mauna Loa since 1958, the yearly average rose from about 316 parts per million in 1959 to about 421 in 2023. Ice cores show pre-industrial levels of about 280 parts per million.

faq.q: What was the London smog of 1952?
faq.a: In December 1952 cold, still air trapped coal smoke over London for five days. Thousands died at the time and later estimates are higher. It led to the Clean Air Act of 1956.
A 1962 book by the American biologist Rachel Carson showing how pesticides such as DDT harmed birds and ecosystems. It helped launch the modern environmental movement.

facts: Keeling began measuring CO2 at Mauna Loa in 1958.
Rachel Carson's Silent Spring was published in 1962.
The first UN conference on the human environment met in Stockholm in 1972.
